items.title: TDK CLI integration: run `mikro-orm migration:up` as a one-shot job in a TDK landscape
items.body:
## Summary

Request for a small, optional way to use `mikro-orm migration:up` together with TDK CLI in a local multi-service setup, or, if that is not wanted here, for guidance on where such a note should live.

## What TDK is

[TDK](https://github.com/tdk-landscape/tdk-cli-core) (Tilt Development Kit, `@tdk-landscape/tdk-cli-core`) is a local multi-service runner. Every service has a `service.json`, and `tdk up <stack>` starts that slice with Docker + Tilt, health-checked boot order and `*.localhost` routing through Traefik. It is not a deploy tool and not a production Compose replacement. Requirements: Docker, Tilt, Bun (for the services it generates).

| Tool | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `mikro-orm migration:up` | ORM and migration CLI |
| `tdk project` / `tdk resource` / `tdk up` | The local landscape: ports, stacks, Docker, Tilt, proxy |

## Why this might fit

`mikro-orm migration:up` is a one-shot command that runs pending migrations and exits, which matches a pre-boot migration job in a local multi-service landscape.

## What I am asking for

- Guidance on the recommended way to run migrations non-interactively in a container. A docs link is enough; I will send a PR if a note is welcome.
- No code change requested.



## Acceptance

- Documented non-interactive migration command and exit-code behavior.
- MikroORM gains no dependency on TDK.
- Optional and additive. TDK is not a required toolchain and does not deploy anything.

## Non-goals

- Replacing your deployment guidance. TDK is local-only.
- Making TDK a dependency of MikroORM.

## Related

Companion issue on the TDK side (the provider or recipe that this depends on): https://github.com/tdk-landscape/tdk-cli-core/issues/268

Disclosure: I'm one of the TDK maintainers, and I drafted this issue with AI assistance. TDK is a young, small project (1.3.x), so I'm keeping the ask small and optional. If this isn't a fit, or isn't wanted in the issue tracker, please just say so and I'll close it.

items.title: A class-level @Check that mentions an enum column is skipped in one diff direction only (PostgreSQL)
Repartitioning a referenced table fails when its PK becomes composite
Generated `down()` drops a partial unique index with `drop constraint`
A runtime-created partition turns `schema:update` into a destructive rebuild
`@Check` constraints on `double precision` columns never diff clean on PostgreSQL
Declare sequence / identity start value and increment in entity metadata
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

There is no way to declare the start value (or increment) of an autoincrement / identity column in entity metadata. Today the only option is raw SQL in a migration (`alter sequence ... restart with 1000`, `alter table ... auto_increment = 1000`).

This has two practical problems:

- Anything built from metadata ignores it: `schema:create`, `schema:refresh`, `orm.schema.refreshDatabase()` in tests. Every test setup has to repeat the raw SQL after the schema is created.
- The value is invisible in the model, so it can drift between environments and nothing reports it.

This was asked in #7158. @B4nan's questions there were: how should it work, what about schema diffing, and should it be respected only when the sequence is created? The proposal below tries to answer them.

The closest thing that works today has a destructive side effect. On Postgres, `generated` is passed through into the DDL, so this creates the column correctly:

```ts
id: { type: 'number', primary: true, generated: 'identity (start with 1000)' }
// create table "thing" ("id" int generated always as identity (start with 1000) not null primary key, ...)
// first insert gets id 1000
```

But introspection reads the column back as plain `identity`, so the very next `getUpdateSchemaSQL()` on an unchanged schema wants to drop and re-add the primary key:

```sql
alter table "thing" drop column "id";
alter table "thing" add "id" int generated always as identity (start with 1000) not null primary key;
```

(Reproduced on 7.2.1 with `@mikro-orm/pglite`.) `generated: 'by default as identity (start with 1000)'` doesn't work either, because only the exact string `'by default as identity'` is special-cased, so it renders as `generated always as by default as identity (...)`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

A `sequence` option on autoincrement properties (decorators and `defineEntity`):

```ts
@PrimaryKey({ sequence: { startWith: 1000, incrementBy: 1 } })
id!: number;

@Property({ autoincrement: true, sequence: { startWith: 10000 } })
ref!: number;
```

Semantics per driver:

| Driver | On create | Diff on change |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, identity (`generated: 'identity'` / `'by default as identity'`) | `generated ... as identity (start with 1000 increment by 1)` | Compare with `information_schema.columns.identity_start` / `identity_increment`, emit `alter table ... alter column ... set start with X set increment by Y` |
| PostgreSQL, `serial` (the default) | `alter sequence "thing_id_seq" start with 1000 increment by 1 restart` right after `create table` (the table is empty at that point) | Compare with `pg_sequences.start_value` / `increment_by`, emit `alter sequence ... start with X increment by Y` |
| MySQL / MariaDB | `create table ... auto_increment = 1000` | None. `information_schema.tables.AUTO_INCREMENT` is "the next AUTO_INCREMENT value", not a declared start, so it can't be diffed. Create-only. |
| SQLite (AUTOINCREMENT tables) | `insert into sqlite_sequence (name, seq) values ('thing', 999)` after create | None. Create-only. |
| MSSQL | `identity(1000, 1)` instead of the hardcoded `identity(1,1)` | None. SQL Server can't alter the identity property of an existing column (the schema helper already works around this). Create-only. |

Answers to the questions in #7158:

1. **Only on create?** Always on create. On Postgres the diff can also compare the declared values with the introspected ones. Per the Postgres docs, `ALTER SEQUENCE ... START WITH` "changes the recorded start value of the sequence. This has no effect on the current sequence value", so the diff never touches existing data. Moving the current value of an existing sequence (`restart`) stays an explicit data-level action in a migration.
2. **Schema diffing:** the start/increment become part of the column's sequence metadata and are compared like defaults or types. Drivers that can't read back a declared start (MySQL, SQLite, MSSQL) skip it in the diff, so there are no spurious migrations.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Raw SQL in a migration: works for migrated databases, but not for `schema:create` / `refreshDatabase()`, and the value isn't visible in the model.
- `generated: 'identity (start with N)'`: creates the right DDL, but every later diff drops and re-adds the PK column (see above).
- `default: raw("nextval('custom_seq')")` with a hand-made sequence: the ORM doesn't create or track the sequence, so it has to be created separately in every environment.

**Additional context**

Prior art:

- EF Core: `modelBuilder.HasSequence<int>("OrderNumbers").StartsAt(1000).IncrementsBy(5)`; SQL Server `UseIdentityColumn(seed, increment)`; Npgsql `HasIdentityOptions(startValue: 100)`
- JPA / Hibernate: `@SequenceGenerator(initialValue = 1000, allocationSize = ...)`
- Drizzle: `pgSequence('name', { startWith: 100, increment: 2 })`, `generatedAlwaysAsIdentity({ startWith: 100 })`

items.title: Backport PostGIS schema diff and snapshot churn fixes to 6.x
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Could the PostGIS schema-comparison fix from #7803 and the snapshot-preservation fix from #7804 be backported to `6.x`?

Both fixes shipped in 7.1.2, but the corresponding changes are absent from the current `6.x` branch. We reproduced the repeated spatial type alterations with 6.6.9. Projects remaining on v6 still encounter both problems:

1. PostgreSQL introspection records `geometry` / `geography` without the `(Point,4326)` type modifier. Migration generation then repeatedly emits `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE geometry(Point, 4326)` and the equivalent geography statement. Whitespace in the modifier also produces a false type difference.
2. `migration:create` saves entity metadata, while `migration:up` and `migration:down` replace the snapshot with database introspection. Equivalent type aliases, index expressions, metadata, and ordering produce large snapshot diffs even when the migrated database matches the saved schema.

### Reproduction

Define an entity with a primary key and these properties on a PostgreSQL database with PostGIS enabled:

```ts
@Property({ type: 'string', columnType: 'geometry(Point, 4326)', nullable: true })
location?: string;

@Property({ type: 'string', columnType: 'geography(Point, 4326)', nullable: true })
geo?: string;
```

1. Generate and apply a migration.
2. Inspect the snapshot: the spatial columns become bare `geometry` and `geography`.
3. Generate another migration without changing the entity.
4. Observe redundant spatial type alterations and changes to the snapshot representation.

The upstream regressions and fixes are already documented in #7798, #7803, and #7804. I am preparing a focused backport PR with v6 regression coverage for both spatial types and snapshot preservation. This request does not include the separate `snapshotOnMigrate` feature from #8039.

### Expected behavior

Preserve spatial type modifiers during introspection, compare equivalent declarations regardless of whitespace, and retain the existing snapshot when the migrated database is semantically equivalent. Real type changes and stale snapshots must still be detected.

### Driver and version

- Driver: `@mikro-orm/postgresql`
- Reproduced version: 6.6.9
- Backport target: current `6.x` (packages currently versioned 6.6.16)
- Node.js: 24.11.0

### Related upstream fixes

- #7803 — PostGIS type-modifier introspection and comparison. Only its spatial-type changes are requested here; the unrelated check-name truncation change is outside this backport's scope.
- #7804 — Preserve snapshots that already match the migrated database.

items.title: Key every user-class lookup by class reference, not class name (follow-up to #8107)
items.body:
Follow-up to #8107.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

#8107 asked for the decorator metadata registry to be keyed by class reference "end to end". The fix that landed covers discovery, and it works: `MetadataStorage.getMetadata` keys by `META_SYMBOL`, `initRelation` resolves through `prop.target` before falling back to a name, and a 166-entity schema discovers cleanly under a bundler that mangles every class name.

The assumption that a class name identifies a class survives everywhere around discovery, and those paths are the ones that fail now. Each one costs a production debugging session to find, and several of the remaining ones fail silently rather than throwing.

How bad the collisions are, in a Next.js 16 Turbopack server build: in one chunk, 129 entity classes occupy 17 distinct minified names. One name, `d`, is shared by 19 entities. All six user-defined `Type` subclasses minify to `a`. Collisions are the default under this bundler, not an edge case.

One relevant detail: MikroORM resolves as an external and ships unminified, so its own classes keep their names. Only **user-supplied** classes get mangled. That scopes the problem — every lookup that keys a user class by name is affected, and nothing internal to the library is.

The confirmed failure is in `EventManager`, which dispatches entity events by name:

```js
// events/EventManager.js:87
return new Set(
  listener.getSubscribedEntities().map((name) => Utils.className(name)),
);

// events/EventManager.js:46
if (entities.size === 0 || !entity || entities.has(entity.constructor.name)) {
  listeners.push(listener[event].bind(listener));
}
```

A subscriber declaring `getSubscribedEntities() { return [Foo] }` received `beforeCreate` for an unrelated entity that mangled to the same name, and crashed reading a relation that entity does not have:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')
     at Object.beforeCreate
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**

An audit of every lookup that resolves a user-supplied class, keying each by class reference or `_id` the way discovery now does, rather than another point fix.

Line numbers are from 7.1.14-dev.10. Only the first row is confirmed by a stack trace; the rest come from reading the source, and I have not built a reproduction for each.

| Location                                                                 | Key                                 | Consequence of a collision                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `events/EventManager.js:46,87`                                           | `entity.constructor.name`           | Subscriber runs for a foreign entity. **Confirmed.**                                                                                                                                                             |
| `EntityManager.js:263` (`addFilter`)                                     | `Utils.className(entity)`           | A global filter registered for one entity applies to another. Silent, and a tenancy filter landing on the wrong entity is a data-exposure bug.                                                                   |
| `EntityManager.js:2119` (cache key)                                      | `Utils.className(entityName)`       | Result cache returns another entity's rows for the same method and query shape. Silent.                                                                                                                          |
| `types/Type.js:57` (`Type.getType`)                                      | `cls.name`                          | Returns a cached instance of a different `Type` subclass. Silent value corruption. Discovery uses `new prop.type()` so it is off that path today, but `getType` is public API.                                   |
| `metadata/MetadataStorage.js:91,102`                                     | `Utils.className`                   | `find()` falls back to the class-name map and `set()` writes it, so the last class registered under a shared name wins every name-based lookup.                                                                  |
| `entity/EntityRepository.js:225`                                         | both sides by name                  | `validateRepositoryType` compares two mangled names, so a wrong-entity call passes validation.                                                                                                                   |
| `metadata/MetadataDiscovery.js:2141`                                     | `Utils.className(cls)`              | `forceEntityConstructor: [A, B]` matches unrelated entities.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `metadata/MetadataDiscovery.js:234`, `metadata/MetadataValidator.js:116` | `prop.type` string vs `m.className` | The "entity not discovered" checks pass on a name match against the wrong entity. `MetadataDiscovery.js:228` already pairs its name check with `discoveredByIdentity`; these two did not get the same treatment. |

Where a name is genuinely load-bearing — STI, `discriminatorMap`, `EntitySchema` string names, `em.find('Foo', …)` — keeping it is fine, documented as requiring stable class names. The distinction I would suggest: a class name is fine for producing a message, and never fine for deciding which class something is.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Dropping `getSubscribedEntities()` and narrowing with `instanceof` inside every hook. This works, but it means the documented filtering API cannot be used at all on a minifying bundler.
- Bundler-side `keep_classnames`, requested in vercel/next.js#96574. Next implemented turbopack client only minification configuration in upcoming 16.4 (vercel/next.js#96578)
- `EntitySchema` with explicit names, as #8107 noted, means abandoning the decorator API across the app.

**Additional context**

`@mikro-orm/core` 7.1.14-dev.10, `@mikro-orm/decorators` legacy decorators, `@mikro-orm/postgresql`, Next.js 16.3.3, Turbopack server build with minification on. Explicit `tableName` on all 166 entities, explicit entity arrays, explicit `type` on every property.

Four of these surfaced in a single migration to a minifying bundler: table-name derivation, `discriminatorMap` resolution, the metadata registry from #8107, and the event manager, with #8107's fix already in place for the last one. Happy to test a canary, and I can share the script that produces the collision census above if a reproduction fixture would help.

items.title: `@mikro-orm/sql`: PostgreSQL check constraint recovery fails on array-typed casts, producing invalid SQL (`ARRAY[...][]`)
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Hello,

When introspecting PostgreSQL check constraints that involve array-typed casts (such as `::text[]`), the cast-stripping regex fails to match the array bracket suffix. This leaves behind an orphaned `[]` in the recovered expression, resulting in invalid SQL that fails with a syntax error when re-emitted as DDL.

**The Root Cause**
In `packages/sql/src/dialects/postgresql/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts`, `getAllChecks()` uses a regex to strip PostgreSQL-added `(expr)::type` casts back to `expr`:

```ts
// packages/sql/src/dialects/postgresql/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts
const def = m ? m[1].replace(/\(([^()]*)\)::\w+/g, '$1') : single ? single[1] : check.expression;

```

Because `\w+` does not match the trailing `[]` of an array type name (such as `text[]`), the replacement consumes `(ARRAY[...])::text` but leaves the `[]` intact.

For example, PostgreSQL stores an `IN` list check on a `varchar` column as:

```sql
CHECK (((mode IS NULL) OR ((mode)::text = ANY ((ARRAY['a'::character varying, 'b'::character varying])::text[]))))

```

During introspection, the expression is stripped down to:

```sql
(mode IS NULL) OR (mode = ANY (ARRAY['a'::character varying, 'b'::character varying][]))

```

**Why This Is Easily Missed**
A simple, standalone `IN` list check on a column is usually intercepted by `getEnumDefinitions()`, which rebuilds the check expression from parsed enum values and discards the string recovery result. However, if the check contains any additional logic (such as an `IS NULL` disjunct or multi-term predicates), it bypasses enum conversion and surfaces this broken expression.

**Impact**
Any workflow that reads existing check constraints and writes them back (such as `schema:update` or `migration:create`) will produce invalid DDL that fails with `42601 syntax error at or near "["` at execution time.

**Suggested Fix**
Allow the regex to optionally match the array bracket suffix `(?:\[\])?`:

```diff
-const def = m ? m[1].replace(/\(([^()]*)\)::\w+/g, '$1') : single ? single[1] : check.expression;
+const def = m ? m[1].replace(/\(([^()]*)\)::\w+(?:\[\])?/g, '$1') : single ? single[1] : check.expression;

```

I would be glad to open a PR for this containing the fix and a regression test under `tests/features/schema-generator/check-constraint.postgres.test.ts`.

### Reproduction

Create a table with a check constraint containing a disjunct:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (
  mode varchar(16), 
  CONSTRAINT chk_mode CHECK (mode IS NULL OR mode IN ('a', 'b'))
);

```

Introspect the table:

```ts
const schema = await DatabaseSchema.create(orm.em.getConnection(), orm.em.getPlatform(), orm.config);
console.log(schema.getTable('t')!.getChecks().find(c => c.name === 'chk_mode')!.expression);

```

**Expected:** `(mode IS NULL) OR (mode = ANY (ARRAY['a'::character varying, 'b'::character varying]))`

**Actual:** `(mode IS NULL) OR (mode = ANY (ARRAY['a'::character varying, 'b'::character varying][]))` *(Note the trailing `[]`)*

Executing DDL with the recovered expression fails with `42601 syntax error at or near "["`.

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

### MikroORM version

7.1.13

### Node.js version

v24.18.0, TypeScript 7.0.2

### Operating system

macOS 27.0 (arm64)

@mikro-orm/sql: PostgreSQL index introspection drops the access method (GIST, GIN, etc.), regenerating them as standard B-trees
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Hello,

When introspecting a PostgreSQL database, the index access method (e.g., `USING gist`, `USING gin`, `USING brin`) is silently dropped unless the index contains functional columns. When the ORM recreates the index, it defaults back to a standard B-tree.

**The Root Cause**
In `packages/sql/src/dialects/postgresql/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts`, `getAllIndexes()` reads the full `pg_get_indexdef()` string. However, it only retains that raw expression if the index contains functional columns:

```ts
// packages/sql/src/dialects/postgresql/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts
const hasFunctionalColumns = index.index_def.some(col => PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.FUNCTIONAL_COL_RE.exec(col))
...
if (hasFunctionalColumns) {
  // Functional-column expression can't be diffed structurally — keep the whole CREATE
  indexDef.expression = index.expression
}

```

For an index over plain columns, the resulting `IndexDef` only retains `columnNames`, `unique`, and `where`. The access method is discarded. Consequently, `getCreateIndexSQL()` emits the default B-tree syntax:

```sql
-- What is actually in the database:
CREATE INDEX idx_org_nodes_path_gist ON public.org_nodes USING gist (path)

-- What is read back and re-emitted by the generator:
CREATE INDEX "idx_org_nodes_path_gist" ON "org_nodes" ("path")

```

**Impact**
This is a silent failure because PostgreSQL happily accepts the re-emitted DDL. It builds a B-tree over the column (e.g., an `ltree` column). However, a B-tree cannot answer the `<@` ancestry queries that the GIST index was explicitly created for, causing every subtree query to silently degrade into a sequential scan.

The exact same regression applies to GIN, BRIN, Hash, and SP-GiST indexes over plain columns. Any workflow that uses `schema:update` or `migration:create` against a database holding these indexes will inadvertently drop and recreate them as B-trees.

**Expected behaviour**

An introspected index should carry enough metadata to be recreated accurately. The ORM should either record the access method on `IndexDef` and emit `USING <am>`, or fall back to keeping the entire `pg_get_indexdef()` string (the same way functional indexes currently do).

**Suggested fix**

The least intrusive fix might be to treat a non-default access method the same way a functional column is treated, preserving the raw expression:

```diff
-const hasFunctionalColumns = index.index_def.some(col => PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.FUNCTIONAL_COL_RE.exec(col))
+const accessMethod = /\busing\s+(\w+)/i.exec(index.expression ?? '')
+const hasFunctionalColumns =
+  index.index_def.some(col => PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.FUNCTIONAL_COL_RE.exec(col)) ||
+  (!!accessMethod && accessMethod[1].toLowerCase() !== 'btree')

```

### Reproduction

You can reproduce this by creating a table with an `ltree` column and a GIST index:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS ltree;
CREATE TABLE t (path ltree NOT NULL);
CREATE INDEX idx_t_path ON t USING gist (path);

```

Then run the following introspection:

```ts
const schema = await DatabaseSchema.create(orm.em.getConnection(), orm.em.getPlatform(), orm.config)
console.log(schema.getTable('t')!.getIndexes())

```

**Expected:** The index definition retains `USING gist`.
**Actual:** The access method is absent, and the generated SQL will recreate it as a standard B-tree.

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

### MikroORM version

7.1.11

### Node.js version

v24.18.0, TypeScript 6.0.3

### Operating system

macOS 27.0 (arm64)

items.title: @mikro-orm/sql: Introspecting a PostgreSQL check constraint unbalances parentheses when the expression contains multiple terms
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Hello,

When introspecting a PostgreSQL database, check constraints with multiple parenthesized terms end up with unbalanced parentheses, resulting in corrupted SQL that fails to parse when reapplied.

**The Root Cause**
In `packages/sql/src/dialects/postgresql/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts`, `getAllChecks()` unwraps `CHECK ((<body>))` and attempts to strip the `(col)::type` casts that PostgreSQL automatically adds. This is done to ensure the recovered expression matches what the user originally wrote:

```ts
// packages/sql/src/dialects/postgresql/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts
const m = /^check \(\((.*)\)\)$/is.exec(check.expression)
const single = m ? null : /^check \((.*)\)$/is.exec(check.expression)
const def = m ? m[1].replace(/\((.*?)\)::\w+/g, '$1') : single ? single[1] : check.expression

```

The issue lies in the cast pattern `\((.*?)\)::\w+`. Because it is not anchored to a balanced group, the lazy `.*?` can still cross a `)` that belongs to an earlier term. As a result, the opening parenthesis it consumes and the closing parenthesis it removes belong to entirely different groups, corrupting the predicate.

**The Symptom**
This corruption occurs when a constraint body has more than one parenthesized term combined with a cast. (A single-term body like `check ((col)::text = 'x')` survives, which is likely why this went unnoticed).

If a user writes this:

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT c CHECK (code IS NULL OR code ~ '^[a-z]+$')

```

PostgreSQL stores it as:

```sql
CHECK (((code IS NULL) OR ((code)::text ~ '^[a-z]+$'::text)))

```

Due to the regex flaw, it is read back by MikroORM as:

```sql
code IS NULL) OR ((code ~ '^[a-z]+$'::text

```

The first `(` and the last `)` of the body are removed, while leaving others mismatched. When `SchemaHelper.createCheck()` emits `check (<that>)`, PostgreSQL rejects it with a `42601 syntax error`.

This breaks any workflow that reads checks out of a database and writes them back (e.g., `schema:update`, or running `migration:create` against an existing schema). Because the generated SQL has unbalanced parentheses, it fails at apply time rather than at generation time, blocking schema migrations.

**Expected behaviour**
The recovered expression should represent the constraint body with the casts removed, but with its parentheses safely intact:

```sql
(code IS NULL) OR (code ~ '^[a-z]+$'::text)

```

**Suggested Fix**
The regex should only strip a cast when the parenthesized group contains no parentheses of its own (which matches the exact shape PostgreSQL emits for a column reference):

```diff
-const def = m ? m[1].replace(/\((.*?)\)::\w+/g, '$1') : single ? single[1] : check.expression
+const def = m ? m[1].replace(/\(([^()]*)\)::\w+/g, '$1') : single ? single[1] : check.expression

```

### Reproduction

Create the table and constraint mentioned above:

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (code text);
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT c CHECK (code IS NULL OR code ~ '^[a-z]+$');

```

Then run the following introspection:

```ts
const schema = await DatabaseSchema.create(orm.em.getConnection(), orm.em.getPlatform(), orm.config)
console.log(schema.getTable('t')!.getChecks()[0].expression)

```

**Expected:** `(code IS NULL) OR (code ~ '^[a-z]+$'::text)`
**Actual:** `code IS NULL) OR ((code ~ '^[a-z]+$'::text`

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

### MikroORM version

items.title: @mikro-orm/entity-generator: Index column order is lost when columns are mapped to relation properties
items.body:
### Describe the bug

Hello,

When generating entities from an existing database, the column order of indexes is not preserved if those columns are part of composite foreign keys mapped to relation properties.

**The Root Cause**
In `packages/sql/src/schema/DatabaseTable.ts`, the `getIndexProperties()` method collects property names into a `Set` and then returns them based on insertion order:

```ts
// packages/sql/src/schema/DatabaseTable.ts
const propBaseNames = new Set<string>();
…
return Array.from(propBaseNames).map(…);   // ~Line 764

```

When physical columns are collapsed into relation properties, the resulting array reflects the order in which the properties were first encountered, not the actual index column order. If a table shares a column across multiple composite foreign keys, several relations might be added to the Set at once. When those columns are encountered again later in the index definition, they are already in the Set and their positions are not updated to match the index.

For example, on our schema, this results in the following mismatch:

```text
uq_role_grants_anchored
  Database actual: (tenant_id, user_id, role_id, org_node_id, coverage)
  Generated order: (org_node_id, role_id, user_id, tenant_id, coverage)

```

*(Another index, `uq_org_nodes_tenant_parent_name`, is reordered in a similar way).*

**Impact**
While this reordering does not break uniqueness constraints, it has two significant side effects:

1. **Performance:** Leading-column selectivity is altered, which dictates whether the query planner can actually use the index efficiently.
2. **Migrations:** Any schema-diff tooling comparing the database `indexdef` against the generated metadata will flag a difference, which blocks the generator's output from being used as a reliable migration source.

### Reproduction

You can reproduce this by creating a table with two composite foreign keys that share their first column, alongside a unique index where the column order differs from the order in which the relations are declared.

```sql
-- Minimal reproduction schema shape:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_probe_anchored
  ON role_grants (tenant_id, user_id, role_id, org_node_id, coverage)
  WHERE org_node_id IS NOT NULL;

```

**Expected:** The generated entity lists the index properties in the exact order defined in the database (`tenant_id, user_id, role_id, org_node_id, coverage`).
**Actual:** The relation properties are emitted in the order they were first collected by the `Set`.

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

### MikroORM version

7.1.10 (@mikro-orm/core, @mikro-orm/postgresql, @mikro-orm/sql)

items.title: @mikro-orm/entity-generator: check constraints are successfully read from the database but never emitted
items.body:
### Describe the bug

I ran into an issue where running the entity generator against a deployed PostgreSQL schema successfully recovers tables, foreign keys, and indexes, but silently drops **all** check constraints.

For context, here is what happens against our schema (16 tables):

| Object | In the database | Recovered by Generator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tables | 16 | 16 |
| Foreign keys (incl. composite) | 34 | 34 |
| Partial indexes | 8 | 7 |
| **Check constraints** | **30** | **0** |

**The Root Cause**
The introspection itself is working perfectly—the checks *are* being read from the database. The drop happens when converting the `DatabaseTable` into `EntityMetadata`.

If you look at `packages/sql/src/schema/DatabaseTable.ts`, the checks are properly stored and exposed by a getter. However, `getEntityDeclaration()` never actually references `getChecks` or `#checks`. Nothing copies them over to the generated entity declaration.

**The Enum Edge Case**
Single-column `IN (...)` checks appear to survive, but they actually don't. A helper identifies them and maps them to an `enum` property. While this preserves the value domain, **the original constraint name and raw expression are lost**. This is a problem because applications often rely on exact constraint names to translate PostgreSQL errors into domain-specific user errors.

Other shapes disappear entirely. For example:

* **Multi-column checks:** `CHECK (permission_mode <> 'all-active' OR system_key IS NOT DISTINCT FROM 'tenant-admin')`
* **Regex checks:** `CHECK (code ~ '^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$')`

**Impact**
If a developer uses the generator's output as the source of truth for migrations, the resulting database will be stripped of all check constraints. This fails silently, and invalid data can be written to the database before anyone notices.

*Side note: `getEntityDeclaration()` already has a great fallback mechanism for complex cases (falling back to a raw expression when things can't be mapped to a simple property). Check constraints simply never reach that logic, so this looks like an oversight rather than an intentional design choice.*

### Reproduction

You can reproduce this by creating a table with a few different check shapes, and then running the generator against it:

```sql
CREATE TABLE probe (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  code varchar(63) NOT NULL,
  mode varchar(16) NOT NULL,
  system_key varchar(63),
  CONSTRAINT chk_probe_code_format CHECK (code ~ '^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$'),
  CONSTRAINT chk_probe_mode CHECK (mode IN ('explicit', 'all-active')),
  CONSTRAINT chk_probe_shape CHECK (mode <> 'all-active' OR system_key IS NOT NULL)
);

```

**Expected:** Three `@Check()` decorators in the generated `Probe` entity.
**Actual:** Zero checks are generated. `chk_probe_mode` is converted to an enum property, but the constraint name is dropped. `chk_probe_code_format` and `chk_probe_shape` vanish completely.

### What driver are you using?

@mikro-orm/postgresql

7.1.10 (@mikro-orm/core, @mikro-orm/postgresql, @mikro-orm/sql)

items.title: Support named parameters in connection.execute
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

In MikroORM v6, the underlying query runner was Knex, which supported named parameter bindings via `knex.raw`. After migrating to v7, this no longer works — `connection.execute` only accepts positional `?` placeholders and an array of values. This makes complex raw queries with many parameters harder to read and maintain:

```ts
await connection.execute(`
    insert into geo_seed (country, region, city)
    values (?, ?, ?)
    on conflict (type, target_id, locale)
        do update set country = excluded.country,
                      region  = excluded.region,
                      city    = excluded.city
`, [country, region, city]);
```

With anonymous placeholders (`?`) you always need to stay on your toes because order is critical — swap two arguments in the array and data goes into the wrong columns. Named parameters (`:country`, `:region`, `:city`) let you simply pass a reference to the function argument: `execute(sql, { country, region, city })`. This is not only more readable but also safer during refactoring, because adding a new field in the middle of the query doesn't require recalculating indices across the entire array.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

```ts
await connection.execute(`
    insert into geo_seed (country, region, city)
    values (:country, :region, :city)
    on conflict (type, target_id, locale)
        do update set country = excluded.country,
                      region  = excluded.region,
                      city    = excluded.city
`, {country, region, city});
```

This can be supported natively in `connection.execute` itself: parse the SQL for `:name` tokens, replace them with positional placeholders, map the object values to the correct order, and execute. No changes to Kysely are needed.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Positional `?` — works today, but error-prone when queries have 10+ parameters or when parameters are added/removed during refactoring.
- `em.getKysely` — great, but overkill for one-off raw SQL migrations/seeds where we already have the query string and just want to bind values safely.
- Manual string replacement — fragile and opens the door to injection if not done carefully.

PostgreSQL dollar-quoted trigger bodies are split at internal semicolons
items.body:
## Describe the bug

PostgreSQL trigger functions generated from entity metadata are dollar-quoted
PL/pgSQL blocks. When the trigger body contains more than one statement,
internal semicolons followed by newlines are treated as migration/schema
statement boundaries.

This affects two public paths:

1. `migrator.createInitial()` returns a split `diff.up`, so the generated
   migration contains separate `addSql()` calls for fragments of one function.
2. `orm.schema.refresh()` executes the same fragments separately and fails with
   `syntax error at or near ";"`.

The generated schema SQL before statement splitting is valid. The split result
from the reproduction is:

```text
create table "items" ("id" serial primary key, "value" int not null default 0);
create or replace function "items_items_increment_after_insert_fn"() returns trigger as $$ begin update items set value = value + 1 where id = NEW.id;
return NEW;; end; $$ language plpgsql;
create trigger "items_increment_after_insert" AFTER INSERT on "items" for each ROW execute function "items_items_increment_after_insert_fn"();
```

But `createInitial().diff.up` contains the function as two entries:

```json
[
  "create or replace function ... where id = NEW.id;",
  "return NEW;; end; $$ language plpgsql;"
]
```

The likely common boundary is the SQL statement splitting that recognizes
single-quoted strings but not PostgreSQL dollar-quoted blocks.

Expected: semicolons/newlines inside `$tag$ ... $tag$` remain part of one SQL
statement for both migration generation and schema execution.

## Reproduction

https://gist.github.com/vkartaviy/bd393135dc77bd8f34fa6cd718e185ac

The gist uses only public `EntitySchema`, `Migrator`, and schema-generator APIs,
pins all MikroORM packages to `7.1.8`, uses pnpm, and includes a PostgreSQL 17
Docker command. `pnpm repro` prints the split migration diff and then reproduces
the `schema.refresh()` syntax error.

## Environment

- Driver: `@mikro-orm/postgresql`
- MikroORM: `7.1.8` (current latest stable)
- Node.js: `v24.14.1`
- pnpm: `11.0.0` in the standalone reproduction
- PostgreSQL: `17`
- OS: macOS `26.5.2`

## Validations

- Read the contributing guidelines and docs.
- Searched open and closed issues for trigger-body, dollar-quoted, PL/pgSQL,
  migration-splitting, and schema-refresh reports.
- Reproduced from a clean standalone pnpm install and dedicated PostgreSQL
  database.

items.body:
### Describe the bug

`migrator.up()` rewrites the migration snapshot from live introspection. If a
migration creates a PostgreSQL trigger with custom SQL, that trigger is copied
into the entity-metadata snapshot even though it is not declared in entity
metadata.

The next `migrator.checkSchema()` returns `true` and `migration:check` asks for a
new migration that drops the trigger. This makes migration-owned PostgreSQL
artifacts and snapshots incompatible.

### Reproduction

Minimal pnpm-only reproduction:

https://gist.github.com/vkartaviy/3607e3da5111d8f659a50f84df6394f0

It uses one `EntitySchema` table and one external statement trigger. The script
creates and drops its own uniquely named PostgreSQL database.

```text
{
  "after": {
    "hash": "46488bed6cae2d389ac7a82ca7c8ffe31c214d36f83be406091862c76d5bfdb2",
    "triggerCount": 1
  },
  "before": {
    "hash": "42bc441236a7512dd41b9b78d738d9de835bf5201578a17f918f25db1d9794e5",
    "triggerCount": 0
  },
  "migrationNeeded": true
}
```

### Expected behavior

Migration-owned triggers that are absent from target entity metadata should
remain in the live database but should not be copied into the entity-metadata
snapshot. ORM-managed triggers declared through `EntitySchema.triggers` must
continue to round-trip normally.

### Additional context

The behavior comes from `Migrator.runMigrations()`: after `up`/`down`, it
introspects the live schema and compares/stores it without distinguishing
metadata-managed triggers from migration-owned external triggers.

A local proof-of-concept filters introspected triggers against
`schemaGenerator.getTargetSchema()` before snapshot comparison/storage. It
keeps the external-trigger snapshot byte-identical with
`checkSchema() === false`, while a separate `EntitySchema.triggers` control also
stays byte-identical and retains its managed trigger.

Versions used:

- MikroORM 7.1.8
- PostgreSQL 17.9
- Node.js 24.14.1
- pnpm 11.13.0

### Describe the bug

`schemaGenerator.skipTables` is honored by `migration:create` but not when `Migrator.runMigrations()` rewrites the migration snapshot from live introspection after `migration:up` / `migration:down`. A table present in the DB but excluded via `skipTables` (e.g. an externally-owned/connector table) leaks into the snapshot after `up()`. The next `migration:create` then diffs the poisoned snapshot against entity metadata and emits a spurious `DROP TABLE` for the skipped table.

### Reproduction

Minimal, self-contained SQLite repro (no external DB): [repro.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30457472/repro.txt)

`npm install && node repro.mjs # exit 1 = bug`

Output on stock 7.1.4:
```
after createInitial(): snapshot contains "foreign_table"? -> false
after up():                     snapshot contains "foreign_table"? -> true
next createMigration() emits DROP TABLE "foreign_table"? -> true
```

### Expected behavior

A table listed in `skipTables` should never appear in the snapshot, regardless of whether it was written by `migration:create` (metadata/target) or by `migration:up`/`down` (introspection). No `DROP TABLE` should be generated for it.

### Root cause / suggested fix

packages/migrations/src/Migrator.ts → runMigrations():
```
const schema = await DatabaseSchema.create(
  this.em.getConnection(), this.em.getPlatform(), this.config,
  undefined, undefined, undefined,
  /* skipTables */ undefined, /* skipViews */ undefined, ctx);
```
`skipTables`/`skipViews` are passed as `undefined`, whereas `SqlSchemaGenerator` passes `this.options.skipTables`/`skipViews` in its own `DatabaseSchema.create` calls. Passing the `schemaGenerator` options through here fixes it (verified against the repro - exit 0).

items.body:
### Describe the bug

For TPT entities with an enum on the base table, the generated schema duplicates the enum's CHECK constraint onto the child tables.

Below is a verbose AI description:

---

  With `inheritance: 'tpt'`, schema generation emits a **base** entity's enum `CHECK` constraint onto the **child** subtype table as well. In TPT the column lives only on the parent table, so the child-table CHECK references a non-existent column and the generated DDL is invalid — `schema.create()` / `migration:up` fails.

  - **sqlite:** `no such column: status`
  - **mssql:** error **207**, `Invalid column name 'status'`

  This is **driver-independent** — the wrong-table constraint is produced in the shared schema layer (`DatabaseSchema.fromMetadata`), so it reproduces on sqlite, mssql, postgres and mysql. The reproduction uses in-memory sqlite per the template guidance.

  ## Entities (defineEntity; same happens with the decorator API)

  ```ts
  enum Status { ACTIVE = 'active', INACTIVE = 'inactive' }

  const PersonSchema = defineEntity({
    name: 'Person', abstract: true, inheritance: 'tpt',
    properties: { id: p.integer().primary(), name: p.string(), status: p.enum(() => Status) },
  });
  class Person extends PersonSchema.class {}
  PersonSchema.setClass(Person);

  const EmployeeSchema = defineEntity({
    name: 'Employee', extends: PersonSchema,
    properties: { department: p.string() }, // no `status` here
  });
  class Employee extends EmployeeSchema.class {}
  EmployeeSchema.setClass(Employee);
  ```

  ## Expected

  The `status` CHECK is emitted on the `person` table only.

  ## Actual

  `getCreateSchemaSQL()` also emits a CHECK on `employee`, whose table has no `status` column:

  ```sql
  create table `person` (`id` integer not null primary key autoincrement, `name` text not null, `status` text check (`status` in ('active', 'inactive')) not null);
  create table `employee` (`department` text not null, `id` integer not null primary key, constraint `employee_id_foreign` foreign key (`id`) references `person` (`id`) on update cascade on delete cascade,
  constraint `employee_status_check` check (`status` in ('active', 'inactive')));
  -- the `employee` table has no `status` column
  ```

  `await orm.schema.create()` then throws `no such column: status`.

  ## Notes

 - The runtime persistence layer already handles this correctly — inserting an `Employee` writes `status` to `person` and only `department`/PK to `employee`.
  - It's only DDL generation that's wrong: `DatabaseSchema.fromMetadata` already restricts TPT child **columns** to `ownProps`, but the **checks** loop iterates `meta.checks` (including inherited entries) without that filter, so inherited enum CHECKs leak onto child tables.

items.title: Triggers dropped from migration snapshot in `getSchemaFromSnapshot()`
items.body:
## Describe the bug

`Migrator.getSchemaFromSnapshot()` drops triggers when deserializing the migration snapshot, even though `DatabaseTable` serializes them. The snapshot round-trip is therefore lossy for any entity that declares a native `@Trigger`: `migration:check` reports "changes detected" on an up-to-date schema, and `migration:create` emits a redundant trigger-recreating migration.

The asymmetry is in `getSchemaFromSnapshot()`. It restores `indexes`, `checks` and `foreignKeys` via their setters, but never calls `setTriggers`, so the triggers written by `DatabaseTable.toJSON()` (`@mikro-orm/sql`, the `sortedTriggers` → `triggers` key) are discarded on read-back:

```js
// @mikro-orm/migrations/Migrator.js — getSchemaFromSnapshot()
if (tbl.foreignKeys) {
  table.setForeignKeys(tbl.foreignKeys);
}
// <-- triggers are present in the snapshot JSON but never restored here
const cols = tbl.columns;
```

Adding the symmetric call fixes it (mirrors `setForeignKeys` directly above):

```js
if (tbl.triggers) {
  table.setTriggers(tbl.triggers);
}
```

I'm happy to submit a PR for this one-line symmetry fix.

## Reproduction

Let me know if reproduction is needed for this issue.

The round-trip can be observed without one:

1. Define an entity with a native `@Trigger`.
2. `await orm.migrator.createInitial(dir)` — writes the initial migration **and the snapshot**, which includes the trigger (`DatabaseTable.toJSON()` serializes it under the `triggers` key).
3. `await orm.migrator.create()` — diffs the (unchanged) metadata against that snapshot.

- **Expected:** the diff is empty.
- **Actual (verified locally on both 7.1.2 and 7.1.4):** the diff contains a spurious `create trigger ...` for the already-snapshotted trigger, because `getSchemaFromSnapshot()` deserialized the snapshot without its triggers. Adding the missing `table.setTriggers(tbl.triggers)` call makes the diff empty again.

## What driver are you using?

`@mikro-orm/postgresql`

## MikroORM version

7.1.2 (confirmed still present in 7.1.4)

## Node.js version

v22.22.0 (TypeScript 5.9.3)

items.title: Add PostgreSQL EXCLUDE constraint support
items.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

MikroORM supports most PostgreSQL constraint types (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `CHECK`), but lacks support for [`EXCLUDE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-EXCLUSION) constraints.

This is typically used to prevent overlapping reservations for a resource directly at the database level:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE room_booking
ADD CONSTRAINT room_booking_no_overlap
EXCLUDE USING gist (
	room_id WITH =,
	tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at, '[)') WITH &&
);
```

## Describe the solution you'd like

I propose adding an entity-level decorator like `@ExcludeConstraint()`. Like `@Check()`, this should tie into schema generation, migrations, introspection, and diffing.

```ts
@Entity()
@ExcludeConstraint({
	name: "room_booking_no_overlap",
	using: "gist",
	expression: (columns) =>
		`${columns.room} WITH =, tstzrange(${columns.startsAt}, ${columns.endsAt}, '[)') WITH &&`,
})
export class RoomBooking {
	// ...
}
```

I am not attached to the exact decorator/API name, but the important part is that MikroORM treats this as a constraint rather than an index.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

- **Abusing `@Index({ expression: "..." })`**: You can use this to emit the `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT` statement, but it breaks schema diffing. Postgres stores the object as a constraint, while MikroORM tracks it as an index. Lifecycle operations fail because MikroORM tries to drop or update an index, but Postgres expects constraint semantics.
- **`@Check()`**: Only evaluates the current row, so it can't compare against other rows.
- **Application-level validation**: Prone to race conditions.

## Additional context

I realize `EXCLUDE` constraints are a somewhat obscure and **PostgreSQL-specific** feature, but they are the canonical Postgres solution for scheduling and reservation overlap rules.

Thank you for the continued good work on MikroORM.

Related docs:

- PostgreSQL [`EXCLUDE` constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-EXCLUSION)
- PostgreSQL [`btree_gist`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree-gist.html)
- MikroORM [`@Index()`](https://mikro-orm.io/docs/indexes)
- MikroORM [`@Check()`](https://mikro-orm.io/docs/decorators#check)

items.title: Partial unique indexes regenerate drop+recreate migration on every migration:create
items.body:
### Describe the bug

When a `@Unique` decorator uses the structured `where` option to declare a partial unique index, the generated PostgreSQL schema diff repeatedly emits a `DROP INDEX` + `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE ...` for that index on every subsequent `migration:create`, even when nothing about the entity has changed.

The root cause appears to be that the snapshot file (`.snapshot-postgres.json`) does not serialize the partial predicate for the index — the entry has `composite: true`, `constraint: false`, `unique: true`, but no `expression` / `where` field.

On the next diff, the schema comparator sees the entity's `where` clause vs. the snapshot's predicate-less index and decides they differ, so it re-emits a churn migration. The next `migration:create` then does the same thing again indefinitely.

### Reproduction


Entity (works for any partial unique combination — `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`, multi-column, etc.):

```ts
@Entity({ tableName: 'subscriptions' })
@Unique({
  name: 'subscriptions_subscriber_course_unique',
  properties: ['subscriber', 'course'],
  where: { course: { $ne: null } },
})
@Unique({
  name: 'subscriptions_subscriber_instructor_unique',
  properties: ['subscriber', 'instructor'],
  where: { instructor: { $ne: null }, course: null },
})
export class Subscription { /* … */ }
```

**Steps:**

1. Add the entity above and run `mikro-orm migration:create`.

   First migration is correct — it drops any prior non-partial index and creates the partial one with the right `WHERE` clause. Apply it. Snapshot is regenerated.

2. Without modifying anything in the entity, run `mikro-orm migration:create` again (e.g. triggered by an unrelated entity change elsewhere).

3. A new migration is generated whose `up()` repeats the exact same `DROP INDEX` + `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … WHERE …` for these partial indexes.

4. Apply it. Run `migration:create` again → the diff comes back a third time. The loop never terminates.

**Expected**

After the partial unique index is created and the snapshot is updated, subsequent `migration:create` runs should consider the index in sync with the entity and emit no diff for it.

**Actual**

The drop+recreate migration is re-emitted on every `migration:create`, polluting the migrations folder with no-op migrations that are byte-for-byte identical to the previous one.

**Snapshot evidence**

After a partial index is created, the relevant entry in `.snapshot-postgres.json` looks like:

```json
{
  "columnNames": ["subscriber_id", "course_id"],
  "composite": true,
  "constraint": false,
  "keyName": "subscriptions_subscriber_course_unique",
  "primary": false,
  "unique": true
}
```

There is no field capturing `WHERE (course_id IS NOT NULL)`.

Compare with a regular `@Unique` (no `where`), which serializes with `"constraint": true` — so the snapshot does differentiate `"partial unique index"` from `"unique constraint"`, it just discards the predicate.

**Workaround**

Going back to the legacy raw form (which the `migration:create` diff seems to treat as opaque) avoids the churn:

```ts
@Unique({
  name: 'subscriptions_subscriber_course_unique',
  properties: ['subscriber', 'course'],
  expression:
    'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX subscriptions_subscriber_course_unique ON public.subscriptions (subscriber_id, course_id) WHERE (course_id IS NOT NULL)',
})
```

…but this defeats the purpose of the structured `where` API and forces hand-written SQL.

items.title: Cli migration with Mongodb
fix(migrations): native enums duplicated per-table in migration snapshot
items.body:
## Bug

Migration snapshot files (`.snapshot-*.json`) include a full copy of all native enum definitions for **every table** in the database, plus once at the schema level. For a database with many tables and many enums, the snapshot file is massively bloated.

## Root cause

In `packages/sql/src/schema/DatabaseSchema.ts`, `addTable()` assigns the schema-level `#nativeEnums` object to each `DatabaseTable` **by reference**:

```ts
// DatabaseSchema.addTable()
table.nativeEnums = this.#nativeEnums; // shared reference to all enums
```

This is intentional for in-memory use (so table-level operations can look up the full enum registry). However, at serialization time two separate `toJSON()` methods both emit the same data:

1. **`DatabaseSchema.toJSON()`** emits `nativeEnums` once at the top level ✓
2. **`DatabaseTable.toJSON()`** emits `nativeEnums` again for **every table** ✗

Since all tables share the same reference (the complete set of enums), a snapshot for a database with 50 tables and 20 enums contains 51 copies of all 20 enum definitions.

## Expected behaviour

Native enums should appear exactly once in the snapshot — at the schema level — where they already live in `DatabaseSchema.toJSON()`.

## Fix

1. Remove `nativeEnums` from `DatabaseTable.toJSON()` — it is redundant since the schema-level copy is canonical.
2. Update `Migrator.getSchemaFromSnapshot()` to wire up the shared reference from schema-level data (`rest.nativeEnums`) rather than from per-table data (`tbl.nativeEnums`), restoring the same shared-reference pattern used during live schema loading.

Old snapshots that still carry per-table `nativeEnums` continue to work because `rest.nativeEnums` (schema level) has always been present and has always contained the same data.

items.title: Clarify migration snapshot lifecycle and post-apply rewrites
items.body:
Related to #7234.

## Problem

The current docs explain snapshots mainly as something written by `migration:create` and then reused by future `migration:create` runs instead of diffing against the current database schema.

That is true, but it does not describe the full lifecycle.

In practice, the snapshot file can represent two different states:

- after `migration:create`, it is written from MikroORM's target schema / metadata
- after `migration:up` or `migration:down`, it can be rewritten from the real database schema via introspection

Because the docs currently focus on the first case, it is easy to assume the snapshot is a stable, reviewable artifact of the generated migrations and always represents the expected database schema 1:1.

## Why this is confusing in teams

A common workflow may look like this:

1. Developer A runs `migration:create` and `migration:up` to test changes
1. Developer A runs `migration:down`, deletes it, makes a small change to entities, and only runs `migration:create`
1. Developer A commits the migration and snapshot without also running `migration:up`
1. Developer B pulls the branch and runs `migration:up`
1. Developer B now gets an unexpected snapshot diff in git

That follow-up diff can contain many changes that are unrelated to any newly authored migration, for example:

- table order changes
- type normalization from database introspection
- index / constraint names changing to match what the database actually produced
- additional fields appearing in column metadata

So even if this behavior is technically intended, it is surprising from a workflow perspective and creates repository churn.

## Concrete example

In my case, applying migrations rewrote the snapshot with changes such as:

- table order shuffling
- `varchar(26) collate "C"` becoming `varchar(26)`
- `timestamptz` becoming `timestamptz(6)`
- `int` becoming `int4`
- unique/index/foreign key metadata being renamed or reshaped

The result was a large snapshot diff after `migration:up` even though no new migration had been created.

## Main request

Could the docs make the snapshot lifecycle more explicit?

In particular, it would help to document that:

- snapshots are not only written by `migration:create`
- `migration:up` and `migration:down` can rewrite them to match the actual database schema
- the snapshot is primarily internal migration state used for diffing/conflict detection, not necessarily a stable human-review artifact
- if teams want the committed snapshot to match the real database state, they may need to run migrations before committing

## Small UX improvement

If this behavior is intentional, a small CLI improvement could help prevent accidental commits of the metadata-derived snapshot state.

For interactive runs, `migration:create` could prompt:

```text
The snapshot may be updated to match the real database schema the next time you run migrations.
Would you like to apply pending migrations now? [Y/n]
```

For non-interactive runs, even a warning would help, for example:

```text
Snapshot was generated from entity metadata and may be rewritten after migration:up/down.
Run pending migrations before committing if you want the snapshot to reflect the real database schema.
```

Even if no prompt/warning is added, I think the docs should set expectations here more clearly.

## Longer-term possibilities

These are not the main request for this issue, but they may be useful future directions.

- Prisma's default development workflow (`prisma migrate dev`) creates and applies migrations together, while `--create-only` is the explicit opt-out for manual editing. That makes the provisional state easier to notice.
- Django also supports creating migrations in sequence, but it reconstructs state from the migration history itself rather than relying on a committed snapshot file with two different meanings.

I am not suggesting MikroORM copy either approach directly. I only mention them as examples that this general usability problem can be approached in different ways in the future.

Thanks.

items.title: diffExpression does not normalize != to <>, causing phantom migration diffs for check constraints in postgres
items.body:
### Describe the bug

PostgreSQL treats `!=` and `<>` as equivalent operators, but internally canonicalizes `!=` to `<>` when storing check constraint definitions. `pg_get_constraintdef()` always returns `<>,` even if the constraint was originally created with `!=`.
The `diffExpression` method in `SchemaComparator` normalizes many PostgreSQL formatting differences (quotes, parentheses, type casts, IN vs = ANY, whitespace, etc.) but does not normalize `!=` to `<>`. This causes `migration:create` to generate a drop + recreate for check constraints on every run, even when the constraint is already correct in the database.

### Reproduction

I can create a reproduction repo later, but this is pretty straightforward.

Define an entity with a check constraint using `!=`:

```ts
const MyEntitySchema = defineEntity({
  name: 'MyEntity',
  tableName: 'my_entities',
  properties: {
    id: p.uuid().primary().defaultRaw('uuidv7()'),
    kind: p.enum(() => MyKind),
    related_id: p.uuid().nullable(),
  },
  checks: [
    {
      name: 'my_check',
      expression: `"kind" != 'foo' OR "related_id" IS NOT NULL`,
    },
  ],
});
```

1. Run `migration:create`: generates the initial migration with the check constraint.
2. Run `migration:up`: applies it.
3. Run `migration:create` again and it generates a new migration that drops and recreates the same constraint:

```ts
this.addSql(`alter table "my_entities" drop constraint "my_check";`);
this.addSql(`alter table "my_entities" add constraint "my_check" check ("kind" != 'foo' OR "related_id" IS NOT NULL);`);
```

4. This repeats infinitely on every `migration:create`.

items.title: TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE] during migrations on Windows due to tinyglobby receiving undefined cwd
items.body:
### Describe the bug

## Describe the bug

When running `npx mikro-orm migration:up` in a NestJS project, the process fails with a TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]. The error originates from tinyglobby (a dependency of @mikro-orm/reflection via ts-morph) attempting to call path.resolve() with an undefined value for cwd.

This issue occurs even if TsMorphMetadataProvider is not explicitly used, as long as @mikro-orm/reflection is present in the dependencies.

The following error:

```
TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "paths[0]" argument must be of type string. Received undefined
    at resolve (node:path:199:9)
    at getOptions (file:///D:/ACODE/mikro-orm-migration-error/node_modules/.pnpm/tinyglobby@0.2.16/node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs:276:66)
    at getCrawler (file:///D:/ACODE/mikro-orm-migration-error/node_modules/.pnpm/tinyglobby@0.2.16/node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs:294:18)
    at Module.globSync (file:///D:/ACODE/mikro-orm-migration-error/node_modules/.pnpm/tinyglobby@0.2.16/node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs:302:30)
    at id (D:\ACODE\mikro-orm-migration-error\node_modules\.pnpm\@mikro-orm+core@7.0.9\node_modules\@mikro-orm\core\utils\fs-utils.js:191:1)
    at Object.id (D:\ACODE\mikro-orm-migration-error\node_modules\.pnpm\@mikro-orm+core@7.0.9\node_modules\@mikro-orm\core\utils\fs-utils.js:191:1)
    at id (D:\ACODE\mikro-orm-migration-error\node_modules\.pnpm\@mikro-orm+core@7.0.9\node_modules\@mikro-orm\core\utils\fs-utils.js:191:1)
    at Array.flatMap (<anonymous>)
    at Object.id (D:\ACODE\mikro-orm-migration-error\node_modules\.pnpm\@mikro-orm+core@7.0.9\node_modules\@mikro-orm\core\utils\fs-utils.js:191:1)
    at Object.id (D:\ACODE\mikro-orm-migration-error\node_modules\.pnpm\@mikro-orm+core@7.0.9\node_modules\@mikro-orm\core\utils\fs-utils.js:191:1) {
  code: 'ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE'
}
```

## Investigation

The dependency tree shows that tinyglobby is introduced via @mikro-orm/reflection:

```
pnpm list tinyglobby --depth 10

mikro-orm-migration-error@0.0.1 D:\ACODE\mikro-orm-migration-error (PRIVATE)
│
│   dependencies:
└─┬ @mikro-orm/reflection@7.0.9
  └─┬ ts-morph@27.0.2
    └─┬ @ts-morph/common@0.28.1
      └── tinyglobby@0.2.16
```

In tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs, the library assumes opts.cwd is always a string or URL:

```js
// node_modules/.pnpm/tinyglobby@0.2.16/node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs
opts.cwd = (
  opts.cwd instanceof URL ? fileURLToPath(opts.cwd) : resolve(opts.cwd)
).replace(BACKSLASHES, '/');
```

resolve(undefined) throws Uncaught TypeError: The "paths[0]" argument must be of type string. Received undefined

In @mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js, the globSync may contain an undefined cwd:

```js
// node_modules/.pnpm/@mikro-orm+reflection@7.0.9_@mikro-orm+core@7.0.9/node_modules/@mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js
return tinyGlobby.globSync(patterns, { ...options, expandDirectories: false });
```

## Fix

### Option 1: Fix in @mikro-orm/core

Add a fallback to process.cwd() when options.cwd is missing in fs-utils.js:

```js
// @mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js
return tinyGlobby.globSync(patterns, {
  ...options,
  cwd: options?.cwd || process.cwd(),
  expandDirectories: false,
});
```

### Option 2: Fix in tinyglobby

tinyglobby should handle undefined cwd by process.cwd():

```js
// tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs
opts.cwd = (
  opts.cwd instanceof URL
    ? fileURLToPath(opts.cwd)
    : resolve(opts.cwd || process.cwd())
).replace(BACKSLASHES, '/');
```

## Additional

Maybe on Windows path.resolve() is strictly typed for the first argument. Switching to ReflectMetadataProvider and removing @mikro-orm/reflection resolves the issue temporarily, but as long as tinyglobby exists in the node_modules, fs-utils.js might still trigger this crash.

### Reproduction

https://github.com/KianmesMoon/mikro-orm-migration-error

Windows

items.title: Calling `orm.migrator.up()` programmatically throws when `tinyglobby` is installed
items.body:
### Describe the bug

## Description

Calling `orm.migrator.up()` programmatically throws when `tinyglobby` is installed in `node_modules` explicitely or as a transitive dependency (e.g. via `@typescript-eslint/typescript-estree`). Migrations work fine when `tinyglobby` is not present, as MikroORM falls back to Node's native `globSync`.

```
TypeError: The "paths[0]" argument must be of type string. Received undefined
 ❯ getOptions node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs:276:66
 ❯ getCrawler node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs:294:18
 ❯ Module.globSync node_modules/tinyglobby/dist/index.mjs:302:30
 ❯ globSync node_modules/@mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js:20:35
 ❯ Object.resolveGlob node_modules/@mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js:76:16
 ❯ Object.resolveGlob node_modules/@mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js:62:26
 ❯ Object.glob node_modules/@mikro-orm/core/utils/fs-utils.js:51:39
```

## Root cause

In `fs-utils.js`, the `glob(input, cwd)` function is called without a `cwd` argument (from `AbstractMigrator.discoverMigrations()`). The `cwd` parameter is then `undefined` and propagated through `resolveGlob` down to:

```js
return tinyGlobby.globSync(patterns, { ...options, expandDirectories: false });
```

The spread `{ ...options }` includes `cwd: undefined`, which overrides tinyglobby's internal default of `process.cwd()`. Node's native `globSync` handles `cwd: undefined` gracefully by falling back to `process.cwd()`, but tinyglobby does not — it calls `path.resolve(undefined)` which throws.

## Suggested fix

Don't forward `cwd: undefined` to tinyglobby — only pass `cwd` when it is defined:

```diff
       globSync = (patterns, options) => {
         patterns = Utils.asArray(patterns).map(p => p.replace(/\\/g, '/'));
+        const tinyOptions = { expandDirectories: false };
         if (options?.cwd) {
-          options = { ...options, cwd: options.cwd.replace(/\\/g, '/') };
+          tinyOptions.cwd = options.cwd.replace(/\\/g, '/');
         }
-        return tinyGlobby.globSync(patterns, { ...options, expandDirectories: false });
+        return tinyGlobby.globSync(patterns, tinyOptions);
       };
```

### Reproduction

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NinjaKinshasa/mikro-orm-v7-tinyglobby-reproduction
npm install
npm run start
```

I was using @mikro/orm core, migrations & postgresql 6.4.0 and the migrations worked just fine. I updated to 6.6.9 and I started noticing the strange behavior. And today I updated to 6.6.10 and the strange behavior persists. If I revert back to 6.4.0, my migrations work again. There are 2 scenarios I have observed so far.

**Scenario 1:**
1. I have an up migration with the command `ALTER TABLE schema.table_name OWNER TO newOwner;`
2. I would run the migrations using IMigrator's up function and it would hang indefinitely.
3. I added logging right before calling `await IMigrator.up({ transaction })` and right after. I see the log before but I do not see it after. The function just hangs.
4. I checked my database and there was a process that was "idle in transaction" which I could tell was the migrations process because the last query the transaction ran was an insert to "mikro_orm_migrations". It didn't seem to commit the migration's transaction ever though.
5. I then tracked it down to the line of SQL code I mentioned above. If I commented that 1 ALTER TABLE line out, my migrations would run successfully.
6. I uncommented and tried adding `isTransactional() => false` to the migration, and it would still hang.
7. What did work was running the migration in isolation (I removed all other migrations to test quicker). It did need the `isTransactional() => false` as well. But it needed both of those things to execute the migration. It needed (1) `isTransactional() => false` and (2) to be ran in isolation with no other migrations. items.title: Upsert in v7 doesn't behave the same as it did in v6
Enum CHECK constraint migration generates invalid SQL when enum values contain single quotes
items.body:
## Bug description

When generating migrations for `@Enum()` properties whose values contain ASCII single quotes (U+0027), the CHECK constraint SQL is invalid because the quotes are not escaped.

For example, an enum value `it's complicated` generates:

```sql
check("status" in ('it's complicated', 'active'))
```

instead of the correct:

```sql
check("status" in ('it''s complicated', 'active'))
```

This causes a PostgreSQL syntax error when running the migration.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Define an entity with an enum containing a single quote:

```typescript
export enum Status {
  ItsComplicated = "it's complicated",
  Active = "active",
}

@Entity()
export class User {
  @PrimaryKey()
  id!: number;

  @Enum({ items: () => Status })
  status!: Status;
}
```

2. Run `npx mikro-orm migration:create`

3. The generated migration contains invalid SQL:

```typescript
this.addSql(`alter table "user" add constraint "user_status_check" check("status" in ('it's complicated', 'active'));`);
```

## Root cause

In `packages/postgresql/src/PostgreSqlSchemaHelper.ts`, the `createTableColumn` method joins enum items without escaping:

```typescript
table.check(
  `${this.platform.quoteIdentifier(column.name)} in ('${column.enumItems.join("', '")}')`,
  {},
  this.platform.quoteIdentifier(checkName),
);
```

**Fix:** escape single quotes by doubling them before joining:

```typescript
table.check(
  `${this.platform.quoteIdentifier(column.name)} in ('${column.enumItems.map(v => String(v).replace(/'/g, "''")).join("', '")}')`,
  {},
  this.platform.quoteIdentifier(checkName),
);
```

## Versions

| Package | Version |
|---------|---------|
| `@mikro-orm/core` | 6.6.3 |
| `@mikro-orm/postgresql` | 6.6.3 |
| Node.js | v22 |
| OS | macOS |

items.title: Stop using `async` when generating TypeScript migrations
items.body:
Thanks for your work on this project. It's definitely the coolest ORM I have ever seen 🙂

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

When I generate a migration with MikroORM (using the default `TSMigrationGenerator`),
the new file triggers the ESLint rule [`@typescript-eslint/require-await`](https://typescript-eslint.io/rules/require-await/). This rule is included in `tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked`, making it widely used.

While the rule is not catching any real bugs in this case, it's not falsely triggered either – as far as I am aware, there is no situation where [`TSMigrationGenerator`](https://github.com/mikro-orm/mikro-orm/blob/53a84dacfa38177fff34cb09053e1b6ee7450347/packages/migrations/src/TSMigrationGenerator.ts) adds an `await` expression to `up()` or `down()`. Additionally, since e.g. the `up()` method is [typed](https://github.com/mikro-orm/mikro-orm/blob/53a84dacfa38177fff34cb09053e1b6ee7450347/packages/migrations/src/Migration.ts#L24) to return `Promise<void> | void`, the migration runner should therefore accept a synchronous function just fine.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Please consider updating [`TSMigrationGenerator.generateMigrationFile`](https://github.com/mikro-orm/mikro-orm/blob/53a84dacfa38177fff34cb09053e1b6ee7450347/packages/migrations/src/TSMigrationGenerator.ts#L8-L24) to remove the `async` keyword from the generated methods and set their return type to a plain `void`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I am aware I can make a custom [`MigrationGenerator`](https://mikro-orm.io/docs/migrations#using-custom-migrationgenerator) for my project. However, I thought that an upstream change could also benefit others. I also wasn't 100% sure that removing `async` wouldn't break anything.

### Additional context

Maybe the keyword is intentional? If yes, perhaps this should just be documented somehow.

I considered that this could be to make the user aware `async` functions are supported by the migrator. In that case, my counterargument is that this can already be inferred from the `Migration` abstract class type definitions; it's not necessary to add this keyword to every migration.

items.title: bigIncrements() generates INT instead of BIGINT in MikroORM v6 + MySQL
items.body:
### Bug Report: `bigIncrements()` generates `INT` instead of `BIGINT` in MikroORM v6 + MySQL

## Description

When using `table.bigIncrements('id')` in migrations with MikroORM v6 + Knex 3.x + MySQL, the generated SQL creates an `INT UNSIGNED` column instead of the expected `BIGINT UNSIGNED` column. This is a regression from MikroORM v5 where the same code correctly generated `BIGINT UNSIGNED`.

## Environment

- **MikroORM Version**: 6.6.8
- **Knex Version**: 3.1.0 (via @mikro-orm/knex@6.6.8)
- **Database**: MySQL 8.0.28
- **Node.js**: v20.5.1
- **Operating System**: macOS / Linux (CI/CD)

### Packages

```json
{
  "@mikro-orm/core": "^6.6.0",
  "@mikro-orm/cli": "^6.6.8",
  "@mikro-orm/knex": "^6.6.8",
  "@mikro-orm/migrations": "^6.6.0",
  "@mikro-orm/mysql": "^6.6.0",
  "@mikro-orm/nestjs": "^6.0.2"
}
```

## Current Behavior

### Migration Code

```typescript
import { Migration } from '@mikro-orm/migrations';

export class MigrationXXXXXXXXXXXCreateCouponConditionsTable extends Migration {
  async up(): Promise<void> {
    const knex = this.getKnex();
    await knex.schema
      .createTable('coupon_conditions', function (table) {
        table.bigIncrements('id'); //  Should create BIGINT, but creates INT
        table.string('discount_code', 100).unique().notNullable();
        // ... other columns
      })
      .then();
  }

  async down(): Promise<void> {
    const knex = this.getKnex();
    await knex.schema.dropTableIfExists('coupon_conditions').then();
  }
}
```

### Actual SQL Generated

```sql
CREATE TABLE `coupon_conditions` (
  `id` int unsigned NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,  -- INT instead of BIGINT
  `discount_code` varchar(100) NOT NULL,
  ...
)
```

### Database Result

```bash
mysql> DESCRIBE coupon_conditions;
+---------------+------------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
| Field         | Type             | Null | Key | Default | Extra          |
+---------------+------------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
| id            | int unsigned     | NO   | PRI | NULL    | auto_increment |  
+---------------+------------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
```

## Expected Behavior

The migration should generate `BIGINT UNSIGNED` as specified by `bigIncrements()`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE `coupon_conditions` (
  `id` bigint unsigned NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,  -- Expected
  ...
)
```

## Comparison with MikroORM v5

### v5 Behavior (Working) 

- **MikroORM**: 5.7.12
- **Knex**: 2.4.2 (via @mikro-orm/knex@5.7.12)
- **Result**: `table.bigIncrements('id')` → `BIGINT UNSIGNED` 

### v6 Behavior (Broken) 

- **MikroORM**: 6.6.8
- **Knex**: 3.1.0 (via @mikro-orm/knex@6.6.8)
- **Result**: `table.bigIncrements('id')` → `INT UNSIGNED` 

## Reproduction Test

### Test 1: Pure Knex (Works Correctly)

```javascript
const knex = require('knex')({ client: 'mysql2' });
const sql = knex.schema
  .createTable('test_table', function (table) {
    table.bigIncrements('id');
  })
  .toSQL();

console.log(sql[0].sql);
// Output: create table `test_table` (`id` bigint unsigned not null auto_increment primary key)
// Correct: BIGINT
```

### Test 2: MikroORM v6 Context (Broken)

```javascript
const { MikroORM } = require('@mikro-orm/mysql');
const config = require('./dist/mikro-orm.config').default;

(async () => {
  const orm = await MikroORM.init(config);
  const knex = orm.em.getConnection().getKnex();

  const sql = knex.schema
    .createTable('test_bigint', function (table) {
      table.bigIncrements('id');
    })
    .toSQL();

  console.log(sql[0].sql);
  // Output: create table `test_bigint` (`id` int unsigned not null auto_increment primary key)
  // Wrong: INT instead of BIGINT

  await orm.close();
})();
```

## Impact

This bug causes **foreign key constraint failures** when:

1. Parent table has `id` with `bigIncrements()` (gets created as INT due to bug)
2. Child table references it with `bigInteger()` (correctly creates BIGINT)
3. MySQL rejects FK with error: `ER_FK_INCOMPATIBLE_COLUMNS`

### Error Example

```
MigrationError: Referencing column 'coupon_condition_id' and referenced column 'id'
in foreign key constraint 'category_coupon_targets_coupon_condition_id_foreign' are incompatible.
```

## Workaround

Currently using `table.integer().unsigned()` instead of `table.bigInteger().unsigned()` for FK columns to match the actual (incorrect) INT type of parent tables.

## MikroORM Configuration

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from '@mikro-orm/mysql';
import { CustomMigrationGenerator } from './core/helpers/migration-generator';

export default defineConfig({
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 33060,
  dbName: 'olscart',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'secret',
  entities: ['dist/**/*.entity.js'],
  entitiesTs: ['src/**/*.entity.ts'],
  debug: true,
  dynamicImportProvider: (id) => require(id),
  migrations: {
    tableName: 'migrations',
    path: 'dist/database/migrations',
    pathTs: 'src/database/migrations',
    snapshot: false,
    generator: CustomMigrationGenerator,
  },
});
```

## Additional Context

- This issue **blocks migration from v5 to v6** for projects relying on `bigIncrements()`
- The bug appears to be in how MikroORM v6 wraps/configures the Knex connection
- Pure Knex 3.1.0 works correctly, so the issue is specific to MikroORM's integration
- CI/CD pipelines fail due to FK constraint errors

## Possible Root Cause

The issue might be related to:

1. MySQL connection configuration in MikroORM v6
2. Knex context initialization in migration runner
3. Schema builder options not being passed correctly from v6 to Knex

## Related Issues

- Knex.js `bigIncrements()` documentation: https://knexjs.org/guide/schema-builder.html#bigincrements
- MySQL data types: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/integer-types.html

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a fresh NestJS + MikroORM v6 project with MySQL
2. Generate a migration using `table.bigIncrements('id')`
3. Run the migration: `npx mikro-orm migration:up`
4. Check the actual column type: `DESCRIBE table_name;`
5. Observe that `id` is `int unsigned` instead of `bigint unsigned`

## Expected Fix

MikroORM v6 should pass through `bigIncrements()` to Knex correctly, resulting in `BIGINT UNSIGNED` columns in MySQL, consistent with:

- Knex.js documentation
- MikroORM v5 behavior
- Developer expectations

items.body:
I’m seeing inconsistent snapshot metadata for the same column depending on which migration command is run.

```ts
@Entity({ tableName: 'Actor' })
export class Actor {
  @PrimaryKey({ type: 'text' })
  id: string;

  @Property({ type: 'text' })
  name: string;
  // ...
}
```

For a `text` primary key (`@PrimaryKey({ type: 'text' })`) on `Actor.id`:

- after creating a migration, snapshot stores `primary: false`
- after running `migration:up`, snapshot changes to `primary: true`

This causes snapshot churn and makes migration snapshots unstable.

I believe this issue is related to that change https://github.com/mikro-orm/mikro-orm/discussions/7210

When I switch to version 6.6.7, it works fine

---

### Versions

- `@mikro-orm/core`: `6.6.8`
- `@mikro-orm/migrations`: `6.6.8`
- `@mikro-orm/postgresql`: `6.6.8`
- Postgres driver: `pg 8.19.0`
- Node: 24
- OS: macOS (Darwin 25.x)

### Reproduction

1. Ensure DB/schema is clean and run existing migrations.
2. Run migration generation (`mikro-orm migration:create`).
3. Inspect `.snapshot-<db>.json` for `Actor.id`.
4. Observe snapshot entry like:

```json
"id": {
  "autoincrement": false,
  "mappedType": "text",
  "name": "id",
  "nullable": false,
  "primary": false,
  "type": "text",
  "unsigned": false
}
```

5. Run `mikro-orm migration:up`.
6. Inspect snapshot again; same column becomes:

```json
"id": {
  "name": "id",
  "type": "text",
  "length": null,
  "precision": null,
  "scale": null,
  "nullable": false,
  "default": null,
  "unsigned": false,
  "autoincrement": false,
  "comment": null,
  "primary": true,
  "unique": false,
  "enumItems": [],
  "mappedType": "text"
}
```

---

### Expected behaviour

Snapshot should be stable and keep consistent PK metadata for `Actor.id` across:
- `migration:create`
- `migration:up`
- `migration:down`

In particular, `primary` should not toggle between `false` and `true` for the same column.

---

### Actual behaviour

`primary` for `Actor.id` flips:
- `false` after migration generation path
- `true` after migration execution path

### Additional inconsistency

Besides `primary` toggling, snapshot column objects also change shape depending on command:

- `migration:create` produces a smaller column object
- `migration:up` rewrites the same column with additional introspected metadata fields
  (`length`, `precision`, `scale`, `default`, `comment`, `unique`, `enumItems`, ...)

So this is both:
1. value inconsistency (`primary: false` vs `true`)
2. structural inconsistency (different metadata keys for the same column)

---

### Additional context/suspicion

From code inspection, snapshot writing after `migration:up/down` uses live schema introspection (`DatabaseSchema.create(...)`), while generation path uses metadata/target schema flow. It looks like these two paths may serialise column PK flags differently for this case (`text` PK + inherited base entity + snapshot refresh).

Could maintainers confirm whether this is expected and, if not, whether it should be normalised so the snapshot format is consistent across both paths?

Thanks!

### Describe the bug

The  latest change to the migrator causes it to always trying to emit snapshot fields when running migrate in production (in our case, inside Docker images). Since the images are read-only, this fails to run the migrator.

Current workaround is setting this in our mikro orm config:

```
snapshot: process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production",
```
